rows.topic: Hoover’s official role in China, 1899
rows.fact: In 1899 Hoover’s official role was technical adviser to Chang Yen-Mao, who paid his salary of $12,500, to survey gold mines in Chang’s realm — not “chief engineer for a mining concern operating at Kaiping” sent by the firm in that title. Moreing had, however, written the British Foreign Office that Hoover would manage gold-mine operations, granted Hoover a percentage of Moreing’s China profits (likely unknown to Chang), and Hoover told his brother he would “have charge” of Bewick, Moreing’s Chinese business. Later, Chang raised his salary, expanded his role at CEMC, and installed him as chief engineer of the newly created Mining Bureau for Chihli, while still refusing to yield control.

rows.topic: Kaiping as the largest foreign property transfer in China; share watering
rows.fact: Whyte, following the scale of the deal, calls it “the largest transfer of property to foreigners in the history of China,” and at trial cites Hoover’s own estimate of “some $50 million worth of high-grade coal.” After the transfer, Moreing registered the English company without Chinese management in the articles, distributed 625,000 of 1 million shares “to himself and his mostly Belgian associates… for no cash consideration whatsoever” (watering the Chinese 375,000), and saddled the company with a £500,000 debenture at 6 percent. rows.topic: Joyce judgment and Hoover’s testimony / destruction of minutes
rows.fact: Chang Yen-Mao v. Moreing (and Bewick, Moreing, and the new CEMC) opened before Mr. Justice Joyce in Chancery on January 17, 1905, and ran sixteen days. Hoover was not a named defendant (the suit was filed May 7, 1903). Under oath he “sang a new tune,” acknowledging the February 19 memorandum as binding and claiming he had tried to uphold joint management — testimony Whyte calls “disingenuous,” given his earlier letters about freeing himself of “any interference from the Chinese board” and calling that board a “farce.” On March 1, 1905, Joyce found for Chang: the memorandum was binding; the defendants’ refusal to honor it was “a flagrant breach of faith”; Joyce was appalled that Hoover “actually took possession of some of the title deeds of the property by main force”; he saw plausible grounds that nearly 425,000 shares had been defrauded; he cleared Chang, “which is more than I can say for some of the other parties concerned.” Hoover later “obtain[ed] and apparently destroy[ed] every copy of the court minutes he could find (one set has survived).”

rows.topic: De Re Metallica translation

rows.topic: Colorado River Compact and Hoover Dam naming

He later records that the dam “had initially been called the Hoover Dam,” that Ickes with FDR’s approval changed it to Boulder Dam, and that “Congress, with Truman’s support, changed it back in 1947.”

rows.topic: SRI’s origin: Swain’s idea, Hoover an early backer; Bechtel as founding director (per Gibson)
rows.fact: The idea of a Stanford research institute was championed in 1925 by chemistry professor Robert E. Swain; “Early supporters included Stanford alumnus and trustee, Herbert Hoover” (then Commerce Secretary). It was tabled in 1930, discussed by a Stanford faculty committee “while meeting at the Bohemian Grove” in 1939, approved in principle by the trustees in February 1946, and incorporated on 6 November 1946, with the trustees electing its directors. Denton’s “Initially conceived by President Hoover” overstates Hoover’s role. Her claim that “Steve was a founding director of SRI” rests on Weldon B. Gibson, SRI: The Founding Years (1981), p. 156, which has not yet been seen.
rows.sources: SRI International, “Corporate History” (archived 22 Jan 2017); SRI, A Heritage of Innovation, ch. 1 (2022); SRI, “SRI takes part in Stanford Research Park 75th Anniversary”; Sally Denton, The Profiteers: Bechtel and the Men Who Built the World (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2016), ch. 10 ¶4 and notes (Gibson, SRI, 117, 156).
rows.disagreeingSources: Sally Denton, The Profiteers: Bechtel and the Men Who Built the World (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2016), ch. 10 ¶4 (“Initially conceived by President Hoover”).
rows.resolution: SRI’s own histories credit Swain with the idea and call Hoover an early supporter (as trustee and Commerce Secretary, not President). Denton gives no source for the Hoover clause. The founding-director claim is attributed to Gibson and is consistent with McCartney’s “principal founders” (CANON-030), but no director list has been seen.
rows.cites: SRI International, “Corporate History” (archived 22 Jan 2017); SRI, A Heritage of Innovation, ch. 1 (2022); SRI, “SRI takes part in Stanford Research Park 75th Anniversary”; Sally Denton, The Profiteers: Bechtel and the Men Who Built the World (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2016), ch. 10 ¶4 and notes (Gibson, SRI, 117, 156).
rows.people: Robert E. Swain; Herbert Hoover; Ray Lyman Wilbur; Atholl McBean; Donald Tresidder; Stephen D. Bechtel Sr.

rows.topic: Contract and Finance Company: ownership, price, and the missing books
rows.fact: The Associates owned the Contract and Finance Company (CFC) through nominal incorporators and paid for its stock with notes, not cash. The Pacific Railway Commission estimated that the Central Pacific paid it “roughly twice the actual cost of construction per mile.” Its books “disappeared, never to resurface” when a congressional investigation threatened. White does not say they were burned or destroyed.

rows.topic: Stanford’s unexplained vouchers and Field’s 1887 ruling
rows.fact: On August 10, 1887, before the Pacific Railway Commission, Stanford could not explain vouchers totalling $783,725.68 (Nov. 9, 1870–Dec. 21, 1880). One voucher was for $171,781.89 for “general expenses” to December 31, 1875. Asked whether any of it was “paid for the purpose of influencing legislation,” he declined to answer. Field’s circuit court refused to compel answers: In re Pacific Railway Commission, 32 F. 241 (C.C.N.D. Cal. 1887). White: the ruling “protected, among others, Stephen Field,” who had received railroad favors.
rows.sources: White, Railroaded (2011) ch8 ¶72–73 (n106–113); 32 F. 241 (CourtListener, verified 2026-11-21)
rows.resolution: Voucher figures and holding verified against the opinion. Stanford’s testimony began July 28 at the Palace Hotel; the voucher exchange was Aug. 10. White cites PRC 5:2461 (ch8 n106) and 7:2465 (ch11 n15) for the same July 28 testimony, so the volume number needs checking.
rows.cites: White, Railroaded (2011) ch8 ¶72–73 (n106–113); 32 F. 241 (CourtListener, verified 2026-11-21)

rows.topic: Pacific Improvement Company as the Associates’ money machine
rows.fact: The four families’ “fortunes were mingled in the Pacific Improvement Company, the descendant of the Contract and Finance Company.” Inside the company it was nicknamed “the Personal Interest Company.” It “took the cream and [left] only the skim milk for the railroads.” It ran up more than $4.5M of debt to the Central Pacific and settled it with bonds that had “no market value.” In 1893 it owed $36M against $90M of claimed assets. Its records are at Stanford (PIC Records 1869–1931).
rows.people: Associates; Mahl; Bretherton

rows.topic: US v. Stanford estate: claim, timing, outcome
rows.fact: Attorney General Olney, “unwillingly and under pressure,” prepared a suit against Stanford’s estate to recover the unpaid Central Pacific loans, relying on California stockholder liability (White). The bill claimed $15,237,000. It was dismissed, and the Supreme Court affirmed on March 2, 1896, holding that the Pacific Railroad Acts imposed no personal stockholder liability: United States v. Stanford, 161 U.S. 412. Stanford died June 21, 1893, owing large sums with most of his estate in trust for the University. Huntington mortgaged nearly all the PIC’s assets to stop Jane withdrawing her quarter share.
rows.sources: White, Railroaded (2011) ch9 ¶103–108 (n150–166); 161 U.S. 412 (LII, verified 2026-11-21); Stanford Law history (suit “toward the end of the year” 1893); ch1 ¶76 (1862 California law made stockholders personally liable for company debts)
rows.disagreeingSources: Draft appendix-b-ledger l.84 and ch/2-13 l.92 compress this to “estate frozen; the federal government sues for $15 million” at Stanford’s death. chronology.md l.77–79 cites Railroaded ch. 11 (it is ch. 9) and adds the jewelry claim, which is not in White.
rows.resolution: The claim was $15.237M, which can be rounded to “$15 million.” The filing date is not given in White (he has it in preparation by 1894; Stanford Law says late 1893), so phrase it as “within months.” Cite ch. 9, not ch. 11.
rows.cites: White, Railroaded (2011) ch9 ¶103–108 (n150–166); 161 U.S. 412 (LII, verified 2026-11-21); Stanford Law history (suit “toward the end of the year” 1893); ch1 ¶76 (1862 California law made stockholders personally liable for company debts)

rows.topic: Insiders, not the corporation, skimmed the land grant
rows.fact: White: George would have been “more correct if he had noted that insiders within the corporations, not the corporations themselves, had skimmed the best lands and townsites for speculative gain.” San Joaquin speculators included E. H. Miller Jr., Central Pacific secretary and Hopkins’s old partner. Huntington called them “land thieves,” yet “both the railroad and the Associates, acting as individual speculators, bought land from them.” Counterweight in the same paragraph: “few of the other top-fifty land purchasers had direct connections with the railroad.” Railroads wanted settlers; “Henry George, Terence Powderly, and other antimonopolists were wrong in thinking that the railroad corporations sought to hold land for speculative profit.”
rows.sources: White, Railroaded (2011) ch11 ¶5 (n3 Orsi 79–81), ¶6 (n4: CPH to Stanford, Dec. 16, 1871; Stanford to CPH, Sept. 30, 1871)
rows.resolution: Insider speculation is documented for named individuals (Miller, Carr, the Associates as individuals). It is not a corporate policy of holding land. Phrase it that way.

rows.fact: “The second-largest purchaser of Western Pacific Railroad lands in Alameda County was William B. rows.topic: Stanford’s UC regent nomination withdrawn (1883)
rows.fact: Gov. George C. Perkins appointed Leland Stanford a UC regent (listed 1882–83). In 1883 the incoming Democratic legislature’s caucus said it would not confirm Perkins’s appointees, and the new governor, George Stoneman, withdrew Stanford’s nomination. Brechin (p. 283) places this just before Leland Jr.’s death in 1884 and the university announcement, and quotes Stanford’s lawyer: “the ambition of an emperor and the spite of a peanut vendor”; the former governor “remembered the insult.” The spite-as-motive link is Brechin’s implication. He cites nothing for the lawyer quote. The “make UC look like a kindergarten” line is local rumor; do not use it as fact.
rows.sources: Gray Brechin, Imperial San Francisco: Urban Power, Earthly Ruin (UC Press, 2006 ed. with new preface) p. 283 ¶; UC, The Centennial of the University of California 1868–1968 (OAC), ‘Regents’; Los Angeles Times, Mar. 4, 1994
rows.disagreeingSources: De Anza ‘County Chronicles’ (rumor of the ‘kindergarten’ remark; says Stanford asked to withdraw)
rows.resolution: Official UC record: Stoneman withdrew the nomination. The 1994 LA Times says Stanford ‘withdrew from consideration.’ Both agree he was never confirmed.
rows.cites: Gray Brechin, Imperial San Francisco: Urban Power, Earthly Ruin (UC Press, 2006 ed. with new preface) p. 283 ¶; UC, The Centennial of the University of California 1868–1968 (OAC), ‘Regents’; Los Angeles Times, Mar. 4, 1994
rows.people: Leland Stanford; George Stoneman; George C. Perkins

rows.topic: Irving M. Scott: Stanford trustee, UC board, UIW, Oregon
rows.fact: Irving Murray Scott (Union Iron Works) was one of the 24 trustees named in Stanford’s Founding Grant (Nov. 11, 1885) and resigned May 11, 1898. Brechin (p. 292) says he “served on the governing boards of both Berkeley and Stanford.” Hammond’s Yale classmate Walker Blaine introduced Scott to Secretary of State Blaine. Scott won the $3M battleship Oregon contract, and Hammond admitted the UIW bid “was not the lowest one received” (p. 128; Hammond’s Autobiography; reliability caveat in canon-fixes §27).

rows.resolution: The trustee role is verified from the Founding Grant and the alumni directory. Hammond’s Autobiography is the only source for the Oregon bid story, and colleagues called it ‘full of lies’ (Brechin ch1 n18).

rows.topic: Founding Grant trustees included the judges of the Sharon–Hill and SP cases
rows.fact: The Nov. 11, 1885 Founding Grant named as trustees Judge Lorenzo Sawyer (first board president), Judge Matthew P. Deady of Oregon and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Stephen J. Field, alongside Charles F. Crocker and Timothy Hopkins. Six weeks later, on Dec. 26, 1885, Deady and Sawyer decided Sharon v. Hill, 26 F. 337 (C.C.D. Cal.), for William Sharon. Brechin (pp. 92–93) quotes Deady (“property and position are in themselves some certain guaranty of truth”) and notes Field’s conflicts in the later Hill litigation (Sharon had lent Field large sums and kept a suite for him). Sawyer also decided Woodruff v. North Bloomfield (Jan. 7, 1884) (Brechin pp. 49–53).

rows.topic: UC regents, Los Alamos and the Bohemian Grove (1940–1952)
rows.fact: Brechin: Rockefeller Foundation grant >$1M for the 184-inch cyclotron. Winthrop Aldrich (Rockefeller son-in-law, Chase chairman) spoke with Lawrence at the Bohemian Club, May 13, 1940 (p. 316). On Sept. 15–16, 1942, Lawrence hosted scientists and brass at the Bohemian Grove; Standard Oil’s Murphree attended (n75), and “From that meeting emerged at least three new cities” (p. 318). “The University of California regents secretly assumed management” of Los Alamos (p. 319), and the arrangement was later formalized (pp. 322–323). Livermore followed in 1952.

rows.topic: Stanford’s 1862 inaugural: anti-Chinese passage
rows.fact: “To my mind it is clear, that the settlement among us of an inferior race is to be discouraged, by every legitimate means. Asia, with her numberless millions, sends to our shores the dregs of her population… the presence of numbers among us of a degraded and distinct people must exercise a deleterious influence upon the superior race.” He offered to concur in “any constitutional action, having for its object the repression of the immigration of the Asiatic races.” In April 1862 the legislature passed the “Act to Protect Free White Labor” ($2.50/month tax). Within two years his CPRR was hiring Chinese.

rows.resolution: Chang’s quotes match the State Library text verbatim (Wikipedia has small wording drift; quote the State Library). The same address attacks land-grant claimants who “dispossess others from a hundred leagues.” That is a land-intent irony for Cardinal.

rows.topic: Crocker family self-dealing through Sisson, Wallace & Co. (labor contracting + commissary)
rows.fact: Sisson, Wallace & Co. (A. W. Sisson, W. H. Wallace, Clark W. Crocker, Charles’s brother) was the CPRR’s largest Chinese labor contractor. It took no fee for supplying men; it was paid through an exclusive right to sell them food and clothing. The payrolls “were delivered to Sisson, Wallace & Co., and the money called for by the rolls was paid to them, and they retained the amounts due them from the Chinamen for supplies, and paid them the remainder.” In June 1866 Sisson received almost $61,000 (~2,000 men). Chang: “especially [lucrative] for the Crocker family, which benefited at each level… he therefore essentially paid himself.” Renamed Sisson, Crocker & Co. after Wallace died (1881).
rows.sources: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (HMH, 2019) p. 114 ¶40 & n.; p. 173 ¶26; Wallace et al. v. Sisson et al. (Cal. Sup. Ct., June 9, 1893), California Unreported Cases vol. 4, 34–47 (text via cprr.net)
rows.resolution: The 1893 court opinion confirms the partnership, the no-fee/commissary model, and payroll routing through the firm. The court dates the firm’s organization to “about 1868”; Chang has a merchandising firm from 1857 (an earlier partnership). The court also names PIC, Western Development and Southern Development as the construction companies; it ties to CANON-059.

rows.topic: The 1867 Chinese strike: dates, scale, demands, end
rows.fact: It began Monday, June 24, 1867: E. B. Crocker’s June 27 letter says “last Monday.” About 3,000 Chinese (Chang; Hopkins: “all”) struck from Cisco to Strong’s Canyon/Truckee, about 30 miles. Demands: $40/month (up from $35, raised from $31 in May) and 10 hours instead of 11, with shorter tunnel shifts. The 8-hour demand appears in the Daily Alta, June 30. The anti-whipping/free-movement demand appears only in the Sacramento Union. The strike ended after about 8 days (around July 1–2). Provisions were stopped: E. B. Crocker credits the Chinese agents; Charles later boasted “I stopped the provisions.” Crocker came with the sheriff and armed men. No concessions were made, but pay quietly rose above $35 for experienced men afterward.
rows.sources: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (HMH, 2019) pp. 147–158 ¶23–51 (Huntington Letters; Meadow Lake Sun June 29, 1867; Daily Alta June 30, 1867); cprr.net (E. B. Crocker to Huntington, June 27, 1867, text); Stanford CRRW Project “1867 Strike”; NPS Golden Spike; LOC business-history guide
rows.disagreeingSources: Ambrose ch. 11 (“late May”); project ledger/appendix-b (June 25); LOC/Stanford CRRW (June 25)
rows.resolution: June 24, 1867 was a Monday. The June 27 letter’s “last Monday” fixes the start at June 24 (NPS and Chang agree). June 25 is a common off-by-one, and “late May” is wrong. Not “high desert”: the strike was in the Sierra.

rows.fact: Stanford wrote to Mark Hopkins (not Huntington) on May 18, 1867. rows.topic: Big Four aim: flood the labor market to lower wages
rows.fact: E. B. Crocker to Huntington, June 27, 1867: “The only safe way for us is to inundate this state and Nevada with laborers… They will all find something to do and a surplus will keep wages low. It is our only remedy for strikes.” Hopkins, June 28: “A Negro labor force will tend to keep the chinese steady, as the chinese have kept the Irishmen quiet.” E. B. Crocker, Sept. 12, 1867: “We want 100,000 chinamen here so as to bring the price of labor down.” Huntington, Oct. 3, 1867: “it would be all the better for us and the state if then should a half million come over in 1868.” In early June 1867 the company sought “5,000 negroes” (Chang says from the federal government).

rows.topic: Crocker and Strobridge under oath (1876): Chinese labor was cheaper and more profitable
rows.fact: Before the Joint Special Committee to Investigate Chinese Immigration (Nov. 1876), Crocker was asked, “Did you make more money out of [employing Chinese] than if you had employed white men?” He answered: “I think I did.” Chinese were paid $35/month (paid through a headman) and spent about 40¢/day at the company store. Strobridge: Chinese labor was “much cheaper. Their board is an important consideration”; “sometimes we did not pay for two months and perhaps more.”

rows.topic: Chinese vs. white wages on the CPRR
rows.fact: In 1864–65 Chinese got $26/month, paying their own board; whites got about 30% more with board included (Chang p. 73). By late 1866 the rate was $31; it was raised to $35 in May 1867. Gilliss (Summit Tunnel): Chinese $31 without board; white foremen $120 with board. Clement: white woodcutters $40 with board vs. Chinese $30 without. Nov. 1866 payroll: Chinese waiters $0.66/day, Chinese laborers $1, white blacksmiths $2.50. Chang paraphrasing E. B. Crocker: Chinese cost about half as much as whites.
rows.sources: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (HMH, 2019) pp. 73, 142–144, 149–150; Gilliss, ASCE Transactions 1872; PRC vol. 6; CSRM MS 79 payroll; Stanford CRRW Project
rows.resolution: Give wage ranges with years; don’t give a single figure.

rows.topic: Chinese deaths on the CPRR: no company count
rows.fact: The CPRR kept no records of deaths and never publicly acknowledged a worker death (Chang p. 222, 227). Company men spoke only of “many” (Clement, Strobridge, Partridge). Gilliss: 15–20 killed by one slide at Tunnel 10. In 1870 the Sacramento Reporter said “perhaps 1,200” sets of bones (~20,000 lb) were shipped; a same-day report said ~50. Chang’s bottom line: “likely well into the hundreds, if not substantially higher.” E. B. Crocker, Jan. 31, 1867: accidents must be planned for so they “will not stop the tracklaying beyond.” Clement: “never cared about them so long as we got the work done.”
rows.sources: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (HMH, 2019) pp. 106–107, 163–164, 222–230 ¶34–62; PRC 6:3217
rows.disagreeingSources: Lake Tahoe 800-drowned legend (no evidence, Chang p. 222)
rows.resolution: Use “hundreds, possibly more,” never “1,200” as fact. The draft’s “did not systematically record” is consistent.

rows.topic: Stanford and federal courtship, 1865–1867
rows.fact: In Aug. 1865 Stanford hosted Speaker Schuyler Colfax and eastern journalists on the line, calling the work “of great magnitude and National importance.” The Six Companies gave a six-hour banquet. Crocker. In July 1867 E. B. Crocker said a federal inspector’s (“Mr. Johnson”) report to the Interior Secretary “will be all that we can ask.”

rows.fact: The Burlingame Treaty (1868) guaranteed free migration between China and the US, protecting the CPRR’s labor pipeline. rows.topic: 1883 Stoneman withdrawal of Stanford’s UC regent nomination
rows.fact: In 1883, after Democrats took the governorship and the legislature, Governor George Stoneman withdrew the unconfirmed recess nomination of Leland Stanford (appointed by Republican Governor George C. Perkins) to the UC Board of Regents. N. Greene Curtis and Isaias W. Hellman, also Perkins appointees, resigned; Hellman was later reappointed and confirmed. Stanford’s service as a UC regent is listed as 1882–83. The official UC centennial history cites the San Francisco Evening Bulletin, February 24, 1883, p. 4, and “Regents Muddle Settled,” Bulletin, February 27, 1883, p. 1, plus the Senate Journal. Those 1883 articles were not independently OCR’d this session (CDNC blocked). A September 17, 1899 San Francisco Call retrospective says the withdrawal, driven by anti–Southern Pacific feeling, “for a time suspended the educational intentions of Governor Stanford, as far as the public knew”; that is 1899 interpretation, not an 1883 quotation. Leland Jr. died March 13, 1884; the Founding Grant is November 11, 1885. Do not treat spite as the documented founding motive.
rows.sources: Centennial of the University of California, 1868–1968, Regents chapter (OAC), citing San Francisco Evening Bulletin, February 24, 1883, p. 4; “Regents Muddle Settled,” San Francisco Evening Bulletin, February 27, 1883, p. 1; Senate Journal. San Francisco Call, September 17, 1899, p. 27. Gray Brechin, Imperial San Francisco (2006), p. 283 (the fact of the withdrawal, not the motive).
rows.disagreeingSources: Brechin p. 283 implies remembered insult as a founding spur, without a footnote.
rows.resolution: The withdrawal is solid. Use the UC centennial and, when retrieved, the 1883 Bulletin. Keep the 1899 Call as later color. Do not make the university a revenge project.

rows.topic: “From the kindergarten up” — not an 1883 Stoneman rumor
rows.fact: No source found ties a “kindergarten” rumor to the 1883 regent-nomination fight. The phrase belongs to 1891-era publicity, and in part to Stanford himself. rows.topic: Sharon v. Hill, December 26, 1885, and the trustee-judge overlap
rows.fact: Sharon v. Hill, 26 F. 337 (C.C.D. Cal. December 26, 1885), was heard “Before SAWYER and DEADY, JJ.” Deady wrote the opinion. The suit, filed October 3, 1883, sought cancellation of an alleged declaration of marriage between William Sharon and Sarah Althea Hill; the court found the declaration and letters forged and granted annulment. Counsel for Sharon included William M. Stewart, who had been named a Founding Grant trustee 45 days earlier (November 11, 1885), on the same instrument as Judges Sawyer and Deady. Field did not sit on this panel. Contemporary press criticism of the trustee conflict was not retrieved this session. Deady’s diary (A Pharisee Among Philistines, 1975) was not opened.

rows.topic: Ross affair: 1900 chronology and the 1901 Committee of Economists report
rows.fact: The 1901 Report of the Committee of Economists (appointed Detroit, December 28, 1900) establishes: Ross missed the usual early-May 1900 reappointment, was reappointed June 2, and on June 5 submitted a resignation effective the end of 1900–01 after learning “Mrs. Stanford does not approve of me as an economist, and does not want me to remain here.” Jordan accepted it on November 12, still praising Ross. On November 14 Ross published a statement attributing the forced resignation to Mrs. Stanford’s dissatisfaction with his views, “particularly coolie immigration and municipal ownership.” Jordan then ended the connection immediately. The committee found the resignation “practically forced by the wish of Mrs. Stanford,” expressed as early as May 1900; it found no evidence of moral defect, incompetence, unfaithfulness, or a November 14 breach of confidence; and it found her objections due “in part at all events” to his silver, immigration, and municipal-ownership views. Jordan’s February 7, 1901, letter in the same report denied that views caused the dismissal and said Ross “was not the proper man for the place he held.” Jane Stanford’s May–December 1900 letters to Jordan and the Ross Affair notebook are in the Jane Lathrop Stanford Papers (located, not fully re-quoted here).

rows.topic: Jordan in Honolulu, March 1905: Waterhouse and the “natural causes” statement
rows.fact: After learning the death would be ruled a poisoning, Jordan sailed to Honolulu. He told the New York Times the trip had “nothing whatever to do with the investigation” (NYT, Mar. 11, 1905). He paid Dr. Ernest C. Waterhouse $350 to review the case. Waterhouse never examined the body, but in a memo prepared for Jordan he was “decidedly not” convinced of poisoning. Jordan's statement cited overeating, exertion and angina, then “hysteria.” The Honolulu physicians publicly rejected it (“It is imbecile to think…”). Jordan replied that the key witness, Dr. Humphris, was “a man without professional or personal standing.” He wrote to Carl S. Smith (Mar. 24, 1905) that he was “morally certain.” The coroner’s jury found strychnine introduced “with felonious intent by some person or persons to this jury unknown.”

rows.topic: Honolulu inquest: dates and verdict
rows.fact: The coroner's jury convened at the Moana Hotel on March 6, 1905, with Judge William F. Stanley sitting for the estate. Chemists testified on March 7. The verdict came the evening of March 9 and was printed March 10: strychnine 'introduced into a bottle of bicarbonate of soda with felonious intent by some person or persons to this Jury unknown.'
rows.sources: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 36 ¶4, ¶20–35, pp. 205–211; Miller 2020 (verdict wording)
rows.disagreeingSources: Earlier ledger placeholder 1905-03-01; ep04 'three weeks away'
rows.resolution: The verdict date is pinned by the book; no source in hand disputes it.
rows.cites: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 36 ¶4, ¶20–35, pp. 205–211; Miller 2020 (verdict wording)

rows.topic: Jordan's Honolulu trip and the natural-causes statement
rows.fact: Jordan and Timothy Hopkins sailed on the S.S. Alameda on March 4 with the detectives Callundan (Morse Agency) and Reynolds (SFPD), and arrived March 10, the day the verdict was printed. Jordan engaged Dr. Ernest C. Waterhouse, who saw neither the death nor the autopsy. The night before the March 15 Honolulu funeral, Jordan and Hopkins issued a statement attributing the death to 'advanced age, the unaccustomed exertion, a surfeit of unsuitable food, and the unusual exposure of the picnic party' (Hawaiian Star, Mar 15). Hopkins: 'we all wish it to be a death from natural causes, don't we?'
rows.sources: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 35 p. 201; ch. 41 pp. 234–235; ch. 42 pp. 240–241 & n. 2; Miller 2020 ch. 9 (Waterhouse $350)
rows.disagreeingSources: chronology.md (old: 'chartered steamer', 'Dr. Ernest Forbes', 'heavy dinner')
rows.resolution: 'Dr. Ernest Forbes' and the 'chartered steamer' have no source. White gives Waterhouse, the scheduled Alameda, and the statement text.
rows.cites: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 35 p. 201; ch. 41 pp. 234–235; ch. 42 pp. 240–241 & n. 2; Miller 2020 ch. 9 (Waterhouse $350)

rows.topic: Household allowance during the estate suit
rows.fact: The 1894 federal suit froze the estate. Jane Stanford kept the university open on the household allowance the court allowed her, an insurance policy and the sale of personal belongings, and cut salaries by 10 percent. The often-repeated claim that the faculty were declared her 'personal servants' is not in White.
rows.sources: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 10 ¶17–19, pp. 58–59; 161 U.S. 412 (1896)
rows.resolution: Resolves the CANON-060 [needs source]. The 'personal servants' device still needs a primary source (Jordan, Days of a Man, or probate records).
rows.cites: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 10 ¶17–19, pp. 58–59; 161 U.S. 412 (1896)

rows.topic: Last words and the 'poisoned again' statement
rows.fact: At the Moana, Room 120, Jane Stanford told Dr. Humphris she had been poisoned again and asked for a stomach pump. Her last words: 'Oh God, forgive me my sins'; 'Is my soul prepared to meet my dear ones?'; 'This a horrible death to die.' From the doctor's entrance to the last spasm was ten minutes.
rows.sources: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 29 ¶10–18, pp. 171–173
rows.disagreeingSources: chronology.md (old composite quote 'This is a horrible death to die... I have been poisoned')
rows.resolution: Single detailed source drawn from inquest testimony. The composite quote in the chronology was wrong.
rows.cites: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 29 ¶10–18, pp. 171–173

rows.topic: Founding Grant and taxes
rows.fact: The Enabling Act (March 1885) and the Founding Grant (Nov 11, 1885) created the university and named its trustees. The university was not tax-exempt at its founding. Jane Stanford wanted a blanket exemption, but Crothers dropped it from the constitutional amendment ratified Nov 6, 1900 (vote 137,667–67,737 per ep04), which let the legislature exempt property used for education.
rows.sources: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 9 ¶24 p. 53; ch. 12 ¶32–34 pp. 71–72
rows.disagreeingSources: chronology.md ('irrevocable, tax-exempt private trust'; Winkler cited)
rows.resolution: Winkler has no Founding Grant material, so that cite was removed. The 8,180 acres and the no-sale clause need a source (the Grant text).
rows.cites: White, Who Killed Jane Stanford? (W. W. Norton, 2022) ch. 9 ¶24 p. 53; ch. 12 ¶32–34 pp. 71–72
rows.people: Leland Stanford; Jane Stanford; George Crothers

rows.topic: Tessier-Lavigne story: tip, first article, board review
rows.fact: Baker, a 17-year-old freshman, was tipped to PubPeer on Nov 1, 2022. He took the images to forensic analysts, among them Elisabeth Bik. His editor Sam Catania said: 'Holy shit. We need to get going.' His first Stanford Daily article ran Nov 29, 2022, the same day the board announced its investigation. Special committee members were named Dec 2. Kirkland's Mark Filip ran the review.
rows.sources: Theo Baker, How to Rule the World (Penguin, 2026) Prologue p. 5; ch. 4 pp. 73–94; ch. 5 pp. 108–109; Notes p. 311
rows.disagreeingSources: Old chronology 'Eighteen-year-old'; ledger placeholder 2022-11-01
rows.resolution: Baker's own account and notes. He was 17 at the time (born January 2005; arrived 'at age seventeen').
rows.cites: Theo Baker, How to Rule the World (Penguin, 2026) Prologue p. 5; ch. 4 pp. 73–94; ch. 5 pp. 108–109; Notes p. 311

rows.fact: The scientific panel found that in the five papers where Tessier-Lavigne was a principal author he 'did not have actual knowledge of the manipulation of research data that occurred in his lab and was not reckless,' but each paper has 'serious flaws in the presentation of research data.' He resigned July 19, 2023.

rows.topic: Fate of the Contract & Finance Co. books (1873)
rows.fact: Before the Wilson Committee hearings (Huntington testified Feb 14, 1873), Hopkins fed the C&F books, 'fifteen sturdy leather-bound volumes', into the furnace in the basement of the CP office. Huntington then told the committee the records had been lost.
rows.sources: Richard Rayner, The Associates (W. W. Norton, 2008) ch. 9 ¶10–11; White, Railroaded ch. 1 ¶80, ¶94 ('disappeared')
rows.resolution: White says the books disappeared; Rayner gives the furnace. They are compatible. Name the burning as Rayner's account.

rows.topic: Stanford's election as governor
rows.fact: Stanford was elected governor of California on September 4, 1861, with nearly 56,000 votes, weeks after the Central Pacific's incorporation.

rows.topic: Cohen's 'emperor … peanut vendor' attack
rows.fact: Alfred Cohen, sued by the Associates for $50,000, defended himself in court and called Stanford 'sullen, remorseless, grand and peculiar, with the ambition of an Emperor and the spite of a peanut vendor'. Crocker then put him back on the payroll.
rows.sources: Richard Rayner, The Associates (W. W. Norton, 2008) ch. 10 ¶9–11; lead-chase CANON-095
rows.resolution: Rayner agrees with CANON-095 on the speaker and the context. He gives no year; 1876 comes from the lead-chase.

rows.topic: 1867 strike: Ambrose's 'late May'
rows.fact: Ambrose puts the strike in 'late May' and cites E. B. Crocker's 'This is the hardest blow we have had' to a letter of May 27, 1867 (n. 34). His own narrative then runs through E. B.'s letters of June 26 and 28 (nn. 37–38) and has Charles confront the strikers on July 1 'after a week of such treatment.' That fits Chang's start date of Monday, June 24, and Chang's dating of the 'hardest blow' letter to June 28.
rows.sources: Chang 2019 pp. 147–151; Ambrose 2000 ch. 11 ¶54–57 (his own internal chronology)

rows.resolution: Ambrose's own July 1 / 'a week' chronology and the June letters contradict his 'late May'. He probably misdated the 'hardest blow' letter.
rows.cites: Chang 2019 pp. 147–151; Ambrose 2000 ch. 11 ¶54–57 (his own internal chronology)

rows.topic: Ten miles in a day, April 28, 1869
rows.fact: Crocker bet Durant $10,000. A derailment on April 27 postponed the attempt. Sunrise was 7:15 a.m. Corinne time; six miles were down by the 1:30 p.m. meal, and ten miles fifty-six feet by 7 p.m. Eight named Irish rail handlers (foreman George Coley) carried 3,520 rails. More than 3,000 Chinese workers unloaded cars, set ties and drove the spikes.
rows.sources: Stephen E. Ambrose, Nothing Like It in the World (Simon & Schuster, 2000) ch. 16 ¶36–49, pp. 347–350; Chang 2019 (Chinese role)
rows.resolution: Ambrose is detailed; Chang agrees on the Chinese role. ep02's 'Seven in the morning, a whistle' was changed to Ambrose's sunrise time.
rows.cites: Stephen E. Ambrose, Nothing Like It in the World (Simon & Schuster, 2000) ch. 16 ¶36–49, pp. 347–350; Chang 2019 (Chinese role)

rows.topic: Promontory: the gold spike and Stanford's miss
rows.fact: The gold spike was set in a pre-drilled hole so it only had to be tapped and could be pulled out again. A telegraph wire was attached to the spike and another to the hammer. 'Stanford swung and missed, striking only the rail. It made no difference.' The wire said 'done!'
rows.sources: Stephen E. Ambrose, Nothing Like It in the World (Simon & Schuster, 2000) ch. 17 ¶40, ¶46–50, pp. 363–365; Chang 2019 (CANON-091)
rows.disagreeingSources: Rayner 2008 ch. 8 ¶29; Winkler 2018
rows.resolution: Two detailed sources against two passing mentions. Keep CANON-091.
